- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.3) or negative (0.0), model tends to overestimate; reduce forecast by 2–5% for next period.  
- After a sharp price spike (forecast > 75.0), model often overshoots and fails to correct; cap forecast at +3–5% above peak or adjust downward if sentiment drops.  
- If sentiment is high (≥0.7) and price is trending up, model may overfit upward momentum; apply mean reversion bias: subtract 1–3% from forecast if sentiment stabilizes or declines.  
- When sentiment is volatile (alternating 0.3–0.7), model exhibits lag; forecast should be adjusted to align with 2–3 day sentiment average, not raw history.  
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates early in the window; reduce first 5–7 days by 1–3% if sentiment is neutral or declining.  
- If sentiment is uniformly low across 18-day history, model tends to ignore downward pressure; apply downward bias of 2–4% to forecast if sentiment remains below 0.4.  
- When sentiment is high but price is flat or declining, model overreacts; reduce forecast by 1–3% if sentiment >0.7 but price moves <1% in last 3 days.
